Univariate GWAS with wgAim

Author

Julian Taylor & Ari Verbyla

Published

August 5, 2026

1 Overview

This vignette demonstrates the complete univariate wgAim GWAS pipeline for a diversity panel evaluated in a single environment. The pipeline has three stages:

  1. Pre-analysis — inspect a raw 0/1/2 marker genotype matrix with checkPanel(), apply quality filters with filterPanel(), and assemble the analysis-ready wgPanel object with primePanel() (including KNN imputation of residual missingness).
  2. Analysis — fit a whole-genome composite marker model and iteratively detect associated markers with gwasAim().
  3. Post-analysis — interrogate, summarise, and visualise the detected associations using the print, summary, and plot methods, and refine peak positions with fineMap().

Throughout the vignette we use the simulated genoGWASraw, mapGWASsim and phenoGWASsim datasets bundled with the package. genoGWASraw and mapGWASsim represent a simulated diversity panel of 200 lines genotyped at approximately 1700 SNP markers across 10 chromosomes (about 170 markers per chromosome, average spacing ~0.9 cM). The panel is generated with AlphaSimR with 50 founder haplotypes via a coalescent (runMacs2), one generation of random mating to produce 200 F1 diverse lines, then a SNP chip actively selected from segregating sites with minor allele frequency (MAF) > 0.15. All shipped markers have F1 MAF > 0.15 (median ~0.32), so the panel is dominated by informative common variants. The resulting kinship matrix \boldsymbol{K} has genuine full-rank structure (off-diagonal SD ~0.085) and captures the half-sib / full-sib relatedness naturally. The raw marker matrix deliberately contains a range of realistic data-quality issues (missingness, monomorphic markers, duplicate lines, duplicate markers and markers absent from the map) so the full pre-analysis pipeline can be exercised. Five QTL were planted at known positions to give ground truth for detection.

See ?phenoGWASsim or the Overview section of the Multivariate GWAS Mapping vignette for a more detailed specification of the phenotype data. In this single-environment vignette we have restricted the analysis to Env1 only.

Requires: ASReml-R V4. The vignette is pre-rendered so no licence is needed to read it. Run the code chunks only if you have ASReml-R installed.

2 Mathematical Framework

The mathematical framework underpinning gwasAim() is essentially identical to that of qtlAim(). Please see the Mathematical Framework section of the Univariate QTL Mapping vignette for the full algorithmic pipeline.

2.1 What’s different in GWAS

Only three things distinguish the GWAS pipeline from biparental interval mapping at the modelling level:

  1. Marker matrix source. qtlAim() operates on virtual mid-interval scores constructed by primeCross(type = "interval") (\lambda-weighted dosages in [-1, +1]). gwasAim() operates on the actual panel markers assembled by primePanel(), coded \pm 1 for the two alleles after the x \mapsto x - 1 shift from raw 0/1/2 counts (heterozygotes at 0). No interval mid-points are constructed; each panel marker is used directly.

  2. Population structure. Diversity panels typically carry both short-range LD and long-range stratification from subpopulations. Both are absorbed by the composite additive term via \boldsymbol{K} in the vm path, so no additional principal- component covariates or kinship correction are required in the base model.

  3. The vm path dominates. Panels almost always satisfy p \gg n (many more markers than lines), so gwasAim() selects the vm formulation automatically. The mbf ridge formulation is available via force = TRUE when n \geq p or for diagnostic comparison.

The exclusion window (argument exclusion.window, default 20) is expressed in the units of the map’s pos column and these are cM for a genetic map, or Mb / kb / bp for a physical map.

3 Data Preparation

The pre-analysis pipeline has three functions applied in sequence:

  1. checkPanel() — pure diagnostic; reports data-quality issues but does not modify the data.
  2. filterPanel() — applies quality thresholds in a principled order.
  3. primePanel() — converts the clean matrix into a wgPanel object and optionally imputes any remaining missing values.
data(genoGWASraw,  package = "wgAim")
data(mapGWASsim,   package = "wgAim")
data(phenoGWASsim, package = "wgAim")

cat(sprintf("Raw geno    : %d lines x %d marker columns\n",
            nrow(genoGWASraw), ncol(genoGWASraw) - 1L))
Raw geno    : 200 lines x 1691 marker columns
cat(sprintf("Map         : %d markers x %d columns\n",
            nrow(mapGWASsim), ncol(mapGWASsim)))
Map         : 1691 markers x 3 columns
cat(sprintf("Phenotype   : %d rows across %d sites\n",
            nrow(phenoGWASsim), nlevels(phenoGWASsim$Site)))
Phenotype   : 2400 rows across 6 sites

A quick look at the raw genotype matrix — a data.frame with an id column followed by one column per marker in 0/1/2 allele-count coding:

3.1 Step 1 — Diagnostic scan with checkPanel()

checkPanel() is a pure diagnostic. It computes summary statistics on the raw matrix, cross-references marker names against the map, and reports data-quality issues but does not modify the data. The results guide the choice of thresholds for the subsequent filterPanel() step.

chk <- checkPanel(genoGWASraw, mapGWASsim,
                   id       = "id",
                   map.id   = "marker",
                   map.chr  = "chr",
                   map.pos  = "pos",
                   encoding = "012")
print(chk)

The printed summary flags every embedded issue: 25 markers in the geno matrix that are absent from the map (unplaceable), 25 markers in the map absent from the geno matrix (the same markers under their original names, before being renamed in the raw matrix), 4 duplicate lines, roughly 50 duplicate marker pairs (the forced pairs plus a small number of natural duplicates from short-range LD), 150 markers with excessive missingness, 5 lines with excessive missingness, 15 monomorphic markers and a MAF distribution consistent with a moderately dense panel. The MAF threshold table makes it easy to preview how many markers would be removed at each conventional cut-off.

3.2 Step 2 — Apply filters with filterPanel()

filterPanel() uses the diagnostics to apply data-quality thresholds in a principled order controlled by a steps argument. The default steps list implements the standard workflow:

  1. Map consistency — drop markers absent from the map.
  2. Marker missingness (default 20%).
  3. Line missingness (default 20%).
  4. Duplicate lines.
  5. Duplicate markers (off by default; enable if desired).
  6. MAF (default 0.05).

The checkPanel object can be piped directly into filterPanel(); all metadata (id column, map field names, encoding) is carried through automatically.

flt <- filterPanel(chk)   # accepts the checkPanel object directly
print(flt)

Filter History
====================================================
  Original : 200 lines,  1691 markers

  Step 1 [Map consistency                    ]: removed 25 marker(s)
  Step 2 [Marker missingness > 20%           ]: removed 150 marker(s)
  Step 3 [Line missingness > 20%             ]: removed 6 line(s)
  Step 4 [Duplicate lines                    ]: removed 3 line(s)
  Step 5 [Duplicate markers                  ]: skipped
  Step 6 [MAF < 0.05                         ]: removed 15 marker(s)
  After    : 191 lines,  1501 markers

  Remaining: 191 lines,  1501 markers

The audit trail shows the effect of each step and confirms the final panel dimensions (typically ~191 lines out of 200 and ~1500 markers out of ~1700 with the default thresholds). Map consistency, the high-missingness marker filter, monomorphic markers and duplicate markers account for most of the marker attrition. The MAF filter is effectively a no-op on this simulated panel since the raw genotypes are already actively sampled at MAF > 0.15 (see the Overview). Line attrition comes from the four seeded duplicate pairs plus five high-missingness lines exceeding the 20% threshold.

3.3 Step 3 — Build the wgPanel with primePanel()

primePanel() converts the filtered matrix into the internal object class used by gwasAim(). It applies the x \mapsto x-1 encoding shift so alleles are represented as \pm 1 (or dosage in [-1, 1]) with heterozygotes at 0, splits the matrix by chromosome, sorts by position within each chromosome and optionally imputes any remaining missing values. The recommended in-package option is chromosome-wise KNN imputation, which uses BLAS-accelerated pairwise distances and pre-sorted neighbour indices to respect the LD structure within each chromosome.

panel <- primePanel(flt, impute = "knn", knn.k = 5)
cat("Class          :", paste(class(panel), collapse = ", "), "\n")
Class          : wgPanel, wgCross, cross 
cat("Chromosomes    :", length(panel$geno), "\n")
Chromosomes    : 10 
cat("Markers total  :",
    sum(sapply(panel$geno, function(el) ncol(el$imputed.data))), "\n")
Markers total  : 1501 
cat("Lines in panel :", nrow(panel$pheno), "\n")
Lines in panel : 191

The wgPanel object stores per-chromosome marker matrices in panel$geno[[ch]]$imputed.data alongside their cM positions in panel$geno[[ch]]$map. A linkMap() call gives a visual summary of the prepared panel:

linkMap(panel, nrow = 1, marker.names = "none") +
  theme(plot.title = element_blank())

4 Base Model — single environment (Env1)

For the single-environment GWAS we subset the phenotype to Env1 and fit a base model that captures the design structure. The trial is a 2-replicate RCBD with row and column plot coordinates. A simple and robust choice is a random-effect model for lines, rows and columns:

env1 <- droplevels(phenoGWASsim[phenoGWASsim$Site == "Env1", ])
env1$Row    <- factor(env1$Row)
env1$Column <- factor(env1$Column)
env1$Rep    <- factor(env1$Rep)

base_env1 <- asreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ Rep,
  random    = ~ id + Row + Column,
  data      = env1,
  na.action = na.method(x = "include"),
  maxit     = 80
)
base_env1 <- update(base_env1)

The line term id captures line-to-line genetic variation prior to any marker modelling; row and column random effects absorb spatial trend across the field layout. Peek at the variance components to confirm all terms are contributing:

summary(base_env1)$varcomp
           component   std.error    z.ratio bound %ch
Row     1.509582e-08          NA         NA     B 0.0
Column  2.965897e-04 0.003780844 0.07844535     P 0.6
id      1.158751e-01 0.020573413 5.63227251     P 0.0
units!R 1.491787e-01 0.015202336 9.81287670     P 0.0

5 Running gwasAim()

gwasAim() takes the converged base model and the wgPanel object. merge.by names the shared line-identifier column (present in both env1 and panel$pheno). The default exclusion.window = 20 acts as a proxy for LD-based exclusion — in this vignette the map is in cM, so 20 means “no other detected marker within 20 cM”:

gwas_env1 <- gwasAim(
  baseModel        = base_env1,
  genObj           = panel,
  merge.by         = "id",
  exclusion.window = 20,
  TypeI            = 0.05,
  trace            = FALSE,
  na.action        = na.method(x = "include"),
  maxit            = 80
)

The engine path (vm or mbf) is selected automatically. With ~191 lines and ~1500 markers after filtering, we sit firmly in the vm regime and the genomic relationship matrix \boldsymbol{K} = \tfrac{1}{p}\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{M}^{\top} is used:

cat("Class              :", paste(class(gwas_env1), collapse = ", "), "\n")
Class              : gwasAim, asreml 
cat("Markers in panel   :", gwas_env1$QTL$n.markers, "\n")
Markers in panel   : 1501 
cat("Significant markers:", length(gwas_env1$QTL$qtl), "\n")
Significant markers: 4

6 Results

6.1 print() — brief narrative

print() reports the significance threshold, panel size and one line per detected marker with its chromosome, name and cM position:

print(gwas_env1, genObj = panel)

GWAS forward selection  TypeI = 0.0500  (1501 markers in panel)

Significant marker on chromosome Chr3: SNP_C03_0128 (110.03 cM)

Significant marker on chromosome Chr2: SNP_C02_0044 (46.00 cM)

Significant marker on chromosome Chr7: SNP_C07_0042 (30.35 cM)

Significant marker on chromosome Chr9: SNP_C09_0068 (60.72 cM)

6.2 summary() — final marker table

summary() collates the final model into a table with one row per detected marker: flanking marker name, cM position, estimated additive effect, p-value, percentage of phenotypic variance explained and LOD score:

summ_env1 <- summary(gwas_env1, genObj = panel)
print(summ_env1)
  Chromosome       Marker dist(cM)    Size  Pvalue Perc.Var   LOD
1       Chr2 SNP_C02_0044    46.00  0.1915   1e-06     18.1  5.35
2       Chr3 SNP_C03_0128   110.03  0.2980  <1e-06     43.7 14.80
3       Chr7 SNP_C07_0042    30.35  0.1583   2e-06     12.3  4.87
4       Chr9 SNP_C09_0068    60.72 -0.1421 3.7e-05      9.9  3.69

Rows are sorted by chromosome and cM position. The planted QTL (in tonnes per hectare per allele substitution) are Chr2 +0.145 and Chr5 −0.145 (both MAIN); Chr7 +0.125 (weak MAIN); Chr3 fading from +0.230 in Env1 down to 0 in Env6; and Chr9 crossing from −0.180 in Env1–Env3 to +0.180 in Env4–Env6. Because we are analysing Env1 in isolation, the two G×E QTL happen to be at their extremes here — Chr3 at its fade peak (+0.230) and Chr9 at its negative crossover extreme (−0.180) — so both come in as the strongest signals, followed by the Chr2 MAIN (+0.145) and the weak Chr7 MAIN (+0.125). The Chr5 MAIN (−0.145) is not detected in this single-environment analysis: with per-site standard errors of roughly 0.03 t/ha the signal-to-noise is on the edge of the LRT threshold, and site-specific residual noise in Env1 was enough to keep it under. This is exactly the kind of borderline main effect that the multi-environment analysis is designed to recover by borrowing strength across sites — see the Multi-Environment GWAS vignette where Chr5 is recovered cleanly alongside the other four. See the roxygen help for ?phenoGWASsim for the shipped marker names and full QTL specification.

7 Visualisation — plot()

Six complementary plot types are available via the type argument of plot.gwasAim(). The default is "manhattan", the classic GWAS display.

7.1 Manhattan plot — type = "manhattan" (default)

A classic Manhattan plot: one point per marker, alternating chromosome backgrounds, significant markers highlighted in sig.col with labels. One facet per forward-selection iteration shows the outlier statistic before each marker is nominated:

plot(gwas_env1, genObj = panel, type = "manhattan", sig.col = "firebrick")

7.2 Genome-wide outlier statistics — type = "outlier"

The outlier plot displays the same genome-wide statistic as line traces faceted by iteration (an alternative to the Manhattan view). Chromosomal regions that persistently carry signal show up as tall peaks across multiple iterations:

plot(gwas_env1, genObj = panel, type = "outlier", sig.col = "firebrick")

7.3 Scaled genome-wide BLUPs — type = "blups"

The BLUPs plot shows the scaled posterior means \tilde{q}_k / \sqrt{|\tilde{v}_k|} at every marker. Markers close to a detected association naturally shrink towards zero as the association absorbs the nearby signal in subsequent iterations:

plot(gwas_env1, genObj = panel, type = "blups", sig.col = "firebrick")

7.4 Allele effects — type = "effects"

The effects lollipop summarises the final set of detected markers. Each marker appears as a lollipop whose head sits at the estimated allele substitution effect ± 1 SE, coloured by which allele is favoured: firebrick when the +1 allele (raw genotype 2) increases yield, steelblue when the −1 allele (raw genotype 0) does. The right panel shows the percentage of variance explained per marker:

plot(gwas_env1, genObj = panel, type = "effects")

7.5 Allele contrast — type = "contrast"

The contrast plot displays the total genetic value for each line against its dosage class (0, 1, 2) at each detected marker. The total genetic value combines three components: the composite genome-wide BLUP, the residual line-level genetic effect, and the summed fixed marker contributions \sum_k \hat{\beta}_k x_{ik}.

This plot requires data, the augmented phenotypic data frame that gwasAim() writes back to the calling environment as <response>.data (here yield.data, which contains the original phenotype columns plus Gomit and the X.<chr>.<idx> dosage columns for each detected marker):

plot(gwas_env1, genObj = panel, type = "contrast",
     data = yield.data, ncol = 2)

7.6 Iteration heatmap — type = "heatmap"

The heatmap gives a compact genome × iteration view, filling each cell with the outlier statistic. This makes it easy to see which chromosomal regions carried persistent signal across iterations:

plot(gwas_env1, genObj = panel, type = "heatmap", sig.col = "firebrick")

7.7 Linkage map overlay — linkMap()

linkMap() overlays the detected markers on the panel map, with marker names annotated on the right and the trait label on the left:

linkMap(gwas_env1, genObj = panel, marker.names = "markers")

8 Iteration Diagnostics — aimTrace()

aimTrace() traces how the LRT statistic and marker effect estimates evolved across the forward-selection iterations. Two diagnostic plots are available.

8.1 LRT trace — plot = "lrt" 

aimTrace(gwas_env1, plot = "lrt", print.out = FALSE)

8.2 Effect stability — plot = "stability"

The stability plot traces each detected marker’s allele effect ± 1 SE across every iteration in which it was present in the model. Effects that remain stable indicate the marker’s contribution is well-identified and not aliased with later-detected markers:

aimTrace(gwas_env1, plot = "stability", print.out = FALSE, ncol = 2)

9 Fine Mapping — fineMap()

fineMap() performs a high-resolution single-marker scan in a window around each detected marker, holding all other detected effects fixed in the model. For gwasAim objects this scans the actual panel markers within ± window cM of the peak (no interpolation), reporting per-marker z-ratio p-values and LOD scores.

We fine-map the two markers detected first in forward selection — these are the strongest signals by construction, since gwasAim() promotes markers greedily by outlier statistic. A 25 cM window with the default exclusion.window = 20 gives good resolution around each peak:

top2 <- head(gwas_env1$QTL$qtl, 2L)
fm <- fineMap(gwas_env1, genObj = panel,
              qtl              = top2,
              window           = 25,
              exclusion.window = 20)

The plot() method draws the LOD profile around each peak. The filled triangle marks the peak fine-map position; the open triangle shows the original coarse-scan position:

plot(fm, ncol = 2)

10 Summary

The complete single-environment GWAS pipeline illustrated in this vignette is:

# 1. Pre-analysis: check -> filter -> prime
chk   <- checkPanel(genoGWASraw, mapGWASsim, id = "id")
flt   <- filterPanel(chk)               # default step list
panel <- primePanel(flt, impute = "knn", knn.k = 5)

# 2. Subset phenotype to the environment of interest
env1  <- droplevels(phenoGWASsim[phenoGWASsim$Site == "Env1", ])
env1$Row    <- factor(env1$Row)
env1$Column <- factor(env1$Column)
env1$Rep    <- factor(env1$Rep)

# 3. Base model (no genomic term)
base_env1 <- asreml(yield ~ Rep, random = ~ id + Row + Column,
                    data = env1, na.action = na.method(x = "include"))

# 4. GWAS forward selection
gwas_env1 <- gwasAim(base_env1, genObj = panel, merge.by = "id",
                     TypeI = 0.05, exclusion.window = 20)

# 5. Results
summary(gwas_env1, genObj = panel)                # final marker table
plot(gwas_env1,    genObj = panel)                # Manhattan (default)
plot(gwas_env1,    genObj = panel, type = "outlier")
plot(gwas_env1,    genObj = panel, type = "blups")
plot(gwas_env1,    genObj = panel, type = "effects")
plot(gwas_env1,    genObj = panel, type = "contrast", data = yield.data)
plot(gwas_env1,    genObj = panel, type = "heatmap")
aimTrace(gwas_env1, plot = "lrt")
aimTrace(gwas_env1, plot = "stability")
linkMap(gwas_env1,  genObj = panel)

# 6. Fine mapping (top two markers in detection order)
top2 <- head(gwas_env1$QTL$qtl, 2L)
fm <- fineMap(gwas_env1, genObj = panel, qtl = top2, window = 25)
plot(fm, ncol = 2)
